## What it was

31 organizations placed across ten workflow stages, from literature grounding
through clinical and regulatory translation. 27 dated developments. 60 linked
sources, each tagged with what kind of evidence it is.

The differentiator was never coverage. It was that the source class travels with
the claim, so a reader can see which entries rest on something a third party
checked and which rest on a homepage.

## Certification

**Verdict: DO NOT PUBLISH — 2 fail, 8 warn.** Published anyway, with the report
beside it.

Failures:

- **[E1]** 32 of 60 sources (53%) carry no date.
- **[E6]** 2 entries dated on the snapshot date were the map re-tagging its own
  cards, counted alongside events in the world.

The warnings are more interesting than the failures, because they are about the
taxonomy rather than the data:

- **[T2]** Mean 4.81 stages per organization out of 10 — the average entry was
  claimed to occupy a third of the lifecycle, which means the taxonomy was not
  discriminating.
- **[T4]** One stage held 23 of 31 organizations (74%). A stage most entries
  qualify for measures label elasticity, not market structure.
- **[T3]** Four organizations were tagged into more than 60% of all stages,
  usually a placeholder for *large incumbent, not researched*.
- **[S3]** No stable IDs, so month-over-month diffs fall back to name matching,
  which cannot distinguish a rename from a removal plus an addition.
- **[E4]** 25 of 31 organizations (81%) had no corroborating source beyond their
  own domain.
- **[E7]** 19 of 27 developments (70%) fell in a single month — a
  recency-weighted search pass, not a trend.
- **[G1]** 7 gap claims over territory the map never surveyed.

Those warnings are why the [stage inclusion tests](../../method.html) exist, and
why no count from either release is quotable until they are applied.

## What r2 fixed

Stable entity and source IDs (**S3**), separated classification changes from
events (**E6**), and added explicit verification status. It did not fix the
undated-source problem — that ratio got worse, from 53% to 87%.
